001.title: Practice laboratory
001.answerIntro: These answers model a defensible explanation. Open-ended exercises have multiple possible strong responses; the criteria below explain what good reasoning should include.

html: A town reports that its library had 12,000 visits last year, that visits rose after Saturday opening, and that the policy was therefore worth its cost. Identify a descriptive claim, a causal inference, and an evaluative judgment. Give one relevant measure missing from the argument.
exercises.answer: Library claims. The count of 12,000 visits is descriptive. A rise after Saturday opening is a chronological association; the claim that extra opening caused the rise requires a comparison. The policy being worth its cost is evaluative. Missing measure: operating costs, unique visitors, learning outcomes or use by groups previously excluded.

html: A friend says, “My uncle smoked every day and lived to ninety-six, so smoking is harmless.” Explain why the personal story does not establish the conclusion. Describe what type of evidence would more directly address the population-level risk.
exercises.answer: Smoking story. One surviving long-lived smoker cannot estimate average risk across a population. Individual variation and selection of memorable cases matter. Large comparative studies with appropriate control of confounding and evidence accumulated across methods address population-level health risks more directly.

html: A city posts a photograph of an empty high street and captions it “Proof our local economy is collapsing.” List three alternative explanations for the image and two additional sources you would check.
exercises.answer: Empty street. Possible explanations include filming early in the morning, temporary roadworks, seasonal closure, weather, or a narrow camera angle. Check local business openings/closures over time, pedestrian counts, tax receipts or independent dated photographs.

html: A researcher says, “This document is a primary source, therefore its description must be accurate.” Evaluate the reasoning and distinguish authenticity, perspective, and factual reliability.
exercises.answer: Primary source. Authenticity asks whether the item is genuine; perspective asks whose interests and viewpoint it expresses; factual reliability asks whether its content is accurate. A contemporary ruler’s boast can be genuine evidence of propaganda without proving every battle claim.

html: A fictional screening system examines 1,000 items, of which 20 are defective. It detects 18 defective items and falsely flags 49 good ones. What fraction of flagged items is actually defective? Why is that not the same as the 90 percent detection rate?
exercises.answer: Screening. There are 18 true positives and 49 false positives, for 67 positive flags. The fraction truly defective is 18/67 ≈ 26.9%. The 90% detection rate is 18/20, the share of real defects successfully found, not the probability a flagged item is defective.

html: After a mayor introduces a training program, employment rises. Design a comparison that would help assess whether the program caused some of the increase. Name two possible confounders.
exercises.answer: Training program. Compare trends among similarly situated eligible people or regions without the program, preferably before and after implementation with careful adjustment. Confounders might include improving national demand, demographic changes, other employment incentives or self-selection by motivated applicants.

html: A headline describes a treatment as “30 percent more effective.” In the study, average scores rose from 10 to 13 points on a 30-point test. Explain what the 30 percent figure describes, and give three other facts needed before recommending the treatment.
exercises.answer: Treatment headline. The mean increases from 10 to 13, which is a 3/10 = 30% relative increase in the particular score. We still need sample size, random assignment or a credible comparison group, uncertainty, side effects, follow-up duration, and whether results generalize beyond the participants.

html: Two news sites repeat an identical claim, and both cite one press release. Does this constitute two independent confirmations? Sketch a better evidence-checking path.
exercises.answer: Copied reporting. Two websites repeating the same press release supply one evidential path, not two independent confirmations. Consult the original report or dataset and a separate relevant analysis or study; verify that cited claims match the source.

html: An unfamiliar research paper reports p = 0.03. Name two conclusions that would be unjustified from that value alone and three additional things worth examining.
exercises.answer: P-value. It does not by itself give the probability that the tested hypothesis is true or the importance/size of an effect. Examine study design, size and uncertainty of the effect, multiplicity of analyses, model assumptions, sample selection and independent evidence.

html: A photograph of an ancient monument appears beside the text “Proof that its builders possessed machines unavailable today.” Construct a fair response that separates observation, missing explanation, and positive evidence for a hypothesis.
exercises.answer: Monument argument. Observation: substantial stones or sophisticated construction exist. Uncertainty: the exact technique may be incompletely reconstructed. Claim: builders had unavailable technology. The last requires independent evidence of that technology, not simply the absence of a fully demonstrated reconstruction.

html: Write a two-minute verification plan for a viral video claiming that a government recently closed a border. Your plan should identify at least one possible misleading use of authentic footage.
exercises.answer: Border-video check. Find the original uploader, date, location, and full clip; compare authoritative border announcements and independent on-scene reporting. The video might depict an older closure, another crossing, an exercise or routine traffic restriction.

html: A politically sympathetic website makes a claim you want to believe. Explain how you would test it using the same standard you would apply to an opponent's claim.
exercises.answer: Sympathetic website. State the claim exactly, investigate provenance, identify reasons it might be wrong, consult relevant independent records, and use the same credibility standards as for a political opponent. A preferred conclusion is not a substitute for evidence.

html: Two researchers disagree about the effect of a policy. One has relevant publications and transparent data; the other is famous but works outside the subject. Explain how their credentials and the substance of their evidence should affect your judgment.
exercises.answer: Experts. Domain-specific experience and transparent methods deserve more weight than celebrity. Consider how each expert addresses the exact question, whether data are available, whether independent work agrees, and whether the disagreement concerns facts, assumptions or values.

html: Essay (400–600 words). Is skepticism always a virtue? Distinguish careful doubt, reflexive opposition, and cynicism; use at least two concrete examples and say what could change your own mind.
exercises.answer: Skepticism essay. Strong essays show careful questioning and evidence-updating, distinguish it from automatic rejection and blanket distrust, and discuss at least two cases. The writer states what would count as disconfirming evidence and avoids applying different standards to favored claims.

html: Essay (400–600 words). Can a statement be factually accurate and still seriously mislead? Discuss an example involving a statistic, image, or historical quotation. Explain how context would change a reader's interpretation.
exercises.answer: Accurate yet misleading. Strong essays explain how a correct quote, selective time window, truncated graph or genuine photograph can mislead without being fabricated. They identify what context was omitted and how restoring it changes the warranted interpretation.

html: Mini-research project. Choose one everyday factual claim. Record the exact wording, trace its origin, consult two genuinely independent relevant sources if available, write one competing explanation, and finish with a confidence level and a remaining question. Give URLs or document titles so somebody else can check your work.
exercises.answer: Mini-research project. Assess whether the exact claim is stated, provenance is traced, sources are independent and relevant, a rival explanation is considered, and the final confidence claim matches the evidence. Reward a well-supported “uncertain” when the available evidence cannot decide the question.

002.title: Practice laboratory
002.answerIntro: These answers model a defensible explanation. Open-ended exercises have multiple possible strong responses; the criteria below explain what good reasoning should include.

html: Separate claims. “Because people are moving away from our town, the government must subsidize local businesses.” Write the stated premise, conclusion, one hidden causal premise and one hidden value premise.
exercises.answer: Stated premise: people are leaving. Conclusion: subsidize local businesses. Hidden causal premise: subsidies will create sufficient local opportunities to change migration choices. Hidden value premise: reducing migration is important enough to justify the fiscal cost and distribution of benefits.

html: Test validity. “If a device is connected to the internet, it uses electricity. This device uses electricity. Therefore it is connected to the internet.” Is the inference valid? Give a counterexample.
exercises.answer: Invalid: affirming the consequent. A device might use electricity without being connected to the internet (for example, an ordinary desk lamp). The premise does not say internet-connected devices are the only devices using electricity.

html: Truth and structure. “All fish live on the Moon. Salmon are fish. Therefore salmon live on the Moon.” Is the argument valid? Is it sound? Explain the difference.
exercises.answer: Deductively valid because the conclusion follows if the premises were true. Not sound: the premise that all fish live on the Moon is false. Truth of premises and validity of the inferential structure are separate tests.

html: Conditional forms. From “If the archive is open, the main entrance is unlocked” and “The main entrance is locked,” what follows deductively, assuming both premises are true? Name the pattern.
exercises.answer: The archive is not open, by modus tollens. Given “If open, then unlocked” and “not unlocked,” one may infer “not open” if the conditional is fully accepted.

html: Necessary or sufficient? A square is a rectangle under standard geometric definitions. Is being a square sufficient for being a rectangle? Is being a rectangle sufficient for being a square?
exercises.answer: Being a square is sufficient for being a rectangle; being a rectangle is not sufficient for being a square. Squares form a subset of rectangles under standard definitions.

html: Classify the inference. “Of the last 50 trains on this line, 45 arrived late. Tomorrow's train will probably arrive late.” Deductive, inductive or abductive? Identify one limitation.
exercises.answer: Inductive prediction. The sample is 45/50 = 90% late, but conditions may change; the observations could come from a disruption period or selected trains. A probabilistic forecast is not a deductive guarantee.

html: Compare explanations. A classroom window is broken. One pupil says a football did it; another says a strong wind did it. What evidence would help distinguish these explanations? Why is the mere existence of broken glass insufficient?
exercises.answer: Investigate trajectory and size of debris, ball marks, weather records, eyewitness reports, nearby activity, and security footage. Broken glass alone is compatible with multiple causes; it does not select the correct one.

html: Find the causal leap. The mayor introduced a new tourism campaign in April, and visits rose in June. Identify three plausible alternatives or confounders to investigate before assigning the increase to the campaign.
exercises.answer: Possible alternatives include seasonal tourist peaks, a new attraction or event, improved transport, and broader regional growth. Also examine measurement changes and whether the campaign began before the rise. A suitable comparison is needed.

html: Clarify the words. A friend says “Country A is the richest in the world.” List three different operational definitions of “richest” and explain why they could produce different rankings.
exercises.answer: Richest might mean highest total GDP, highest GDP per person, or highest median household wealth or income. Population size, price levels and inequality make the rankings differ.

html: Facts and values. “The new bypass would reduce travel times by ten minutes, so it should be built.” Name a missing empirical consideration and a missing value or policy consideration.
exercises.answer: Empirical: total travel-time benefits, construction costs, traffic diversion, safety effects or environmental impact. Value/policy: whether such gains outweigh loss of land, budget trade-offs or unequal impacts.

html: Reconstruct fairly. A proposed policy would restrict car through-traffic at certain hours. Rewrite the straw man “Supporters want to ban cars forever” as a criticism that fairly addresses the actual proposal.
exercises.answer: A fair criticism: “The proposed peak-hour restriction could reduce customer access and shift congestion to neighboring streets; what evidence and exemptions will address those effects?” This critiques the actual policy.

html: Assess the speaker. A scientist has a financial interest in a product they recommend. Explain why that information may matter without treating it as proof that the product is ineffective.
exercises.answer: A financial conflict could bias testimony or the evidence selected, so disclose it and check independent research. It does not logically prove that the recommendation or product is false.

html: Spot the false choice. “Either the state owns every hospital or healthcare cannot be accessible.” Give at least two possible institutional alternatives and identify what would need evidence.
exercises.answer: Alternatives could include publicly financed care delivered by nonprofit providers, mixed public-private systems, regulated private providers, or publicly owned hospitals with varying payment arrangements. Compare access, quality, cost and coverage empirically.

html: Test a slope. “If the school allows one deadline extension, deadlines will become meaningless.” Identify two questions that would determine whether this is a serious forecast or an unsupported slippery-slope claim.
exercises.answer: Ask whether exceptions are limited by written criteria and whether one exception has historically led to others despite safeguards. Identify a plausible institutional mechanism and evidence, rather than assuming disaster follows automatically.

html: Distinguish universals. A friend says “Every successful author writes for six hours daily.” What would one counterexample show? Would it also refute “Most successful authors write daily”?
exercises.answer: One verifiable successful author with a different schedule refutes “every.” It does not refute “most,” which requires evidence about how common each schedule is among a relevant representative group.

html: Recognize circularity. “The website is accurate because it publishes correct information; we know it publishes correct information because it is accurate.” Identify the missing independent test.
exercises.answer: The premises restate the conclusion. Independent checks could include documented corrections, transparent evidence, comparison to original records, or a verified accuracy study of a defined sample of articles.

html: Numbers and assumptions. A hypothetical €6,000 solar installation is said to pay back in 15 months because the monthly electricity bill is €400. State at least four conditions required for this shortcut to hold. Calculate simple payback if verified net annual savings were €1,200.
exercises.answer: Shortcut requires the full €400 monthly bill to disappear sustainably, no unavoidable charges, accurate generation timing, zero extra expenses, and no relevant financing/maintenance losses. At €1,200 net yearly savings, simple payback = €6,000 / €1,200 = 5 years; this omits the time value of money and later variability.

html: Extended essay: disagreement without distortion. Write 400–600 words about one controversial public policy. Present the strongest argument for it, the strongest argument against it, the key factual uncertainties, the competing values, and a provisional conclusion stating what could change your mind.
exercises.answer: Essay rubric: present the policy fairly; distinguish descriptive facts, causal expectations and value judgments; give the strongest objection; identify what data would shift the conclusion; avoid rhetorical distortion. A sophisticated answer may remain uncertain.

html: Extended case study: an empire's decline. Choose an empire studied in the book's later chapters. Draft a causal map distinguishing long-term conditions, immediate triggers, decisions, and consequences. Explain which parts are well evidenced and which remain debated.
exercises.answer: Historical essay rubric: separate persistent structural pressures from a proximate trigger, identify human decisions and pathways, compare rival interpretations, and indicate whether each claim rests on primary records, archaeological evidence or later scholarship. Do not force monocausal certainty.

html: Conversation exercise. Ask a friend to make a claim about history, sport, economics or technology. Without interrupting, identify its conclusion and one unstated premise; then restate it charitably and ask one open question. Reflect afterward on whether the exchange became clearer.
exercises.answer: Conversation reflection: identify an accurately stated conclusion and premise, check whether the other speaker confirms the summary, ask a nonleading question, and note whether the exchange became clearer rather than more combative.

003.title: Practice laboratory
003.answerIntro: These answers model a defensible explanation. Open-ended exercises have multiple possible strong responses; the criteria below explain what good reasoning should include.

html: Denominators. Town A reports 75 road accidents in a population of 15,000; Town B reports 120 in a population of 40,000. Calculate reported accidents per 1,000 residents in each town. Which has the higher total, and which has the higher per-resident rate? Name one reason the rates are not enough to establish which roads are safer.
exercises.answer: Town A: 75/15,000 × 1,000 = 5 accidents per 1,000 residents. Town B: 120/40,000 × 1,000 = 3 per 1,000. B has more accidents in total; A has the higher population-normalized rate. Rates per resident omit traffic volume, exposure and severity.

html: Percentages and percentage points. A survey's support for a proposal moves from 40 percent to 48 percent. What is the percentage-point increase, and what is the percentage increase relative to the original support?
exercises.answer: 48% − 40% = 8 percentage points. Relative to 40%, 8/40 = 20% increase. Neither description tells us whether this change exceeds the survey’s uncertainty.

html: Reversing a fall. The price of a hypothetical asset falls 30 percent. By what percentage must it subsequently rise from the new price to regain its starting value? Show the calculation using a starting value of €100.
exercises.answer: €100 becomes €70 after a 30% fall. Regaining €30 from €70 requires €30/€70 = 42.857%, or about 42.9%. Opposite changes use different denominators.

html: Independent outcomes. You toss two fair coins independently. Calculate the probability of two heads, exactly one head, and at least one head. Why are “two heads” and “exactly one head” mutually exclusive?
exercises.answer: Four equally likely outcomes: HH, HT, TH, TT. P(two heads)=1/4=25%; P(exactly one head)=2/4=50%; P(at least one head)=3/4=75%. The first two categories cannot occur on the same pair of flips.

html: Conditional cards. From a standard 52-card deck, one card is drawn at random. Calculate P(king | face card) and P(face card | king). Give the denominators explicitly.
exercises.answer: Among 12 face cards, 4 are kings: P(king | face card)=4/12=1/3. Among 4 kings, all are face cards: P(face card | king)=4/4=1.

html: Why independence matters. Three batteries each have an assumed 5 percent probability of failure during a particular period. Calculate the probability all three fail if their failures are independent. Then explain one plausible reason the independent-failure assumption could be wrong.
exercises.answer: Under independent failures, (0.05)^3 = 0.000125 = 0.0125%. A shared manufacturing defect, temperature, flood, or power system might correlate failures, invalidating direct multiplication.

html: The warning signal. In 20,000 transactions, 2 percent are fraudulent. An alert system identifies 80 percent of fraudulent transactions and falsely flags 4 percent of legitimate transactions. Build a four-cell count table and calculate the proportion of flagged transactions that are fraudulent. Round your final result to one decimal place.
exercises.answer: Fraud: 20,000×0.02 = 400. Legitimate: 19,600. True positives: 400×0.8 = 320; missed fraud: 80. False positives: 19,600×0.04 = 784; legitimate not flagged: 18,816. Flagged total: 1,104. Fraud among flags: 320/1,104 ≈ 29.0%.

html: Change the base rate. Recalculate the previous question's proportion of actual fraud among alerts if the fraud rate were 10 percent, with the same detection and false-positive rates. Explain why the answer changes.
exercises.answer: Fraud: 2,000; legitimate: 18,000. True positives: 1,600; missed fraud: 400; false positives: 720; legitimate not flagged: 17,280. Flagged total: 2,320. Fraud among flags: 1,600/2,320 ≈ 69.0%. The higher fraud base rate changes how informative an alert is.

groups.title: B. Risk, uncertainty and decision making

html: Absolute versus relative. An event rate in a hypothetical study falls from 12 percent to 9 percent over the same time period. Give the absolute reduction in percentage points, the relative reduction in percent, and the simple number needed to treat under the study's assumptions. Round NNT up to a whole person.
exercises.answer: Absolute risk reduction: 12% − 9% = 3 percentage points (0.03). Relative reduction: 3/12 = 25%. NNT under the stated conditions: 1/0.03 = 33.33; round up to 34 people. Time horizon and comparability are needed.

html: Expected outcome. A one-time offer has a 40 percent chance of earning a €60 net gain and a 60 percent chance of producing a €25 net loss. Calculate its expected monetary value. Would a positive answer settle whether everyone should take the offer? Explain.
exercises.answer: Expected net value = 0.40×€60 + 0.60×(−€25) = €24 − €15 = +€9. Positive average is not decisive for someone who cannot afford the downside, faces a one-time choice, or doubts the inputs.

html: Festival decision. An organizer expects a 60 percent chance of dry weather. Without cover, a dry day earns €800 net and a wet day loses €500 net. With cover, the organizer earns €350 net regardless of weather. Which option has the higher expected monetary return? Would your recommendation necessarily be identical for an organizer who cannot afford a €500 loss?
exercises.answer: No cover: 0.60×€800 + 0.40×(−€500) = €280. With cover: €350 for either weather outcome. Covered event is €70 higher in expected money and avoids the simplified negative outcome. A cash-constrained organizer may have stronger grounds to choose cover.

html: Insurance and resilience. A hypothetical €50,000 loss has a probability of 0.4 percent in one year. What is the expected monetary loss? Give two defensible reasons a risk-averse household might pay a premium above that expected loss for suitable insurance.
exercises.answer: Expected monetary loss = 0.004×€50,000 = €200. A household could pay more than €200 to avoid an unaffordable catastrophic loss, stabilize the budget, or protect future housing and credit. Actual insurance terms still matter.

html: The travel-time trap. Journey A takes 35 minutes every day. Journey B takes 25 minutes half the time and 45 minutes half the time. Compare their average travel times. Which would you choose if you must arrive within 40 minutes? State the assumptions of your answer.
exercises.answer: Mean A = 35 min. Mean B = 0.5×25 + 0.5×45 = 35 min. For arrival within 40 min, Route A always arrives in this model and Route B arrives in time half the time. Actual traffic or departure times may change the comparison.

html: Two uncertain situations. A fair die roll and a decision about a new market are both uncertain. Explain why they are not the same kind of probability problem and name the evidence that would improve the business forecast.
exercises.answer: A fair die has an explicit symmetric model, while a new market requires uncertain demand, competition, seasonality, prices, and changing customer behavior. Improve the forecast with representative sales histories, pilot launches, competitor research, and sensitivity analysis; retain model uncertainty.

html: A spectacular headline. A politician says crime “surged by 100 percent” after reports rose from three incidents to six in a small area. Give two questions that would make the claim easier to evaluate without denying that the arithmetic is correct.
exercises.answer: Ask what period and geographic unit the six reports describe and what happened in comparable periods. Check changes in reporting practices and population. A 100% rise from three to six is numerically correct, but may be a volatile small count.

html: A very large poll. A website survey collects 100,000 voluntary responses saying users prefer Product A over Product B. Explain why the large sample does not, by itself, make the result representative of the population of all customers.
exercises.answer: Voluntary site respondents may disproportionately consist of loyal or dissatisfied users; the sampling frame may exclude many customers. Large n reduces random variation within the collected set but does not automatically fix who chose or was able to respond.

html: Streaks. A fair coin lands heads five times. What is the probability of tails next if the next toss is independent? What would change your answer if the coin might be biased?
exercises.answer: P(tails next)=50% if the coin is fair and the next toss independent. If coin fairness is uncertain, a long, well-recorded series of outcomes could change the model or estimate; five heads alone are limited evidence.

html: Forecast calibration. A forecaster makes 200 forecasts of 70 percent rain on comparable days. Rain occurs on 100 of those days. Is that outcome consistent with approximate calibration at 70 percent? Explain without deciding the entire quality of the forecaster from one probability category.
exercises.answer: Among 70% forecasts, rain on 100/200 = 50% of cases, far below 70%; under a suitable independence model this is not consistent with good calibration of this forecast category. Still assess all probability bands, event definitions, sample selection, and other forecasting qualities.

html: Compounding. Starting from €500, calculate the balance after three years at a hypothetical fixed annual growth rate of 4 percent, with gains reinvested and no costs. Then calculate the total price increase after two successive annual inflation rates of 8 percent and 5 percent. Round monetary amounts to two decimals and the inflation total to one decimal.
exercises.answer: €500×(1.04)^3 = €562.432 ≈ €562.43. Two successive inflation rates compound: (1.08×1.05 − 1)×100 = 13.4%, not 13.0%. These are hypothetical constant rates.

html: Essay — the confident claim. Write 250–400 words analyzing a statement such as “This company has never failed to deliver, so the next delivery is guaranteed.” Separate the observed evidence from the prediction, discuss sample size and dependence, and identify what further evidence would help. End with a more defensible conclusion.
exercises.answer: Essay rubric: name the actual sample of deliveries and period, show that zero observed failures does not guarantee zero future failure, consider dependence and process change, identify source quality, and state a calibrated conclusion (“observed performance has been strong; future failure remains possible”).

html: Essay — an informed disagreement. Two people debate whether to invest a town's emergency fund in a higher-return but more volatile asset. Write 250–400 words presenting the strongest case for each side, distinguishing expected monetary gain from downside risk and public obligations, and explaining what you would need to decide responsibly.
exercises.answer: Essay rubric: present expected return, variance, liquidity, loss tolerance, opportunity cost, and duty to preserve public emergency services; argue both sides fairly. A strong conclusion discusses safeguards, investment policy, and evidence needed rather than maximizing headline return alone.

html: Your personal numerical checklist. Find a real numerical claim from a news story, advertisement, or public statement. Record the claim's exact wording and source. Answer: What is the event? What is the denominator? What is the baseline and time period? Is the number conditional or relative? What uncertainty is admitted? What would change your judgment? Do not invent missing facts; label them “not reported.”
exercises.answer: Claim audit rubric: reproduce the original wording accurately, supply the source, name numerator/denominator/baseline and time frame if available, identify whether conditional risk or relative change is implied, and mark missing details explicitly. Avoid invented certainty.

004.title: Practice laboratory
004.answerIntro: These answers model a defensible explanation. Open-ended exercises have multiple possible strong responses; the criteria below explain what good reasoning should include.

html: Century identification. Identify the centuries for 44 BCE, 1 CE, 476 CE, 1453 CE, and 1908 CE. Show how you know, especially for 44 BCE.
exercises.answer: 44 BCE = first century BCE (100–1 BCE). 1 CE = first century CE (1–100). 476 CE = fifth century (401–500). 1453 CE = fifteenth century (1401–1500). 1908 = twentieth century (1901–2000). For BCE, the fifth century is 500–401 BCE; lower numbers are later.

html: Crossing the era boundary. How many years elapse from the start of 2 BCE to the start of 2 CE in standard historical notation? Explain the role of the missing year zero.
exercises.answer: Three years: beginning of 2 BCE to 1 BCE (one), to 1 CE (two), to 2 CE (three). The conventional historical year sequence has no year zero.

html: A calendar puzzle. An event is dated October 1917 in a Russian source and November 1917 in a Western European account. Give a plausible historical reason both dates could refer to the same event. What would you check before declaring either source wrong?
exercises.answer: Julian (“Old Style”) and Gregorian (“New Style”) calendars can place the same 1917 Russian event in October and November respectively. Check whether the sources date an event by the calendar used locally and when each jurisdiction adopted the Gregorian calendar.

html: Event or process? Classify each statement primarily as a dated event, longer process, or consequence: (a) an independence proclamation; (b) a decades-long spread of literacy; (c) diplomatic recognition after a declaration. Explain why the categories are analytical tools rather than perfect boxes.
exercises.answer: (a) Event; (b) long-running process; (c) consequence of the event and a diplomatic process in its own right. Classifications depend on the research question and scale.

html: Periodization. Give two reasons why “medieval” is less helpful as a universal label for every region of the world than as a specified regional historical period.
exercises.answer: The period label is derived largely from European historical frameworks and turning points; other regions had different political, cultural, and economic chronologies. It can also conceal regional variation and continuity.

html: Source type depends on the question. A modern historian uses a 1750 textbook's account of ancient Rome. When is that book a secondary source, and when could the same book become a primary source?
exercises.answer: Secondary evidence for ancient Rome because it interprets earlier evidence; primary evidence for eighteenth-century ideas about Rome, education, classical learning, or the historiography of that period.

html: The photograph. A photograph shows hundreds of people in a square, with a handwritten note reading “The whole nation supported the new government.” State three things the photograph might help establish and three claims it cannot establish alone.
exercises.answer: With verified date and provenance it might document a crowd, some visible signs, and features of the square. Alone it cannot show every participant’s beliefs, national opinion, or exactly what occurred outside the frame; the caption itself needs checking.

html: The minister's report. A report written by a minister during a harvest crisis says, “Our relief program has satisfied every village.” List four questions a historian should ask before treating the statement as evidence that aid actually reached everyone.
exercises.answer: Ask who prepared it and for whom, what “satisfied” means, whether village-level delivery receipts or accounts corroborate it, what disfavored recipients report, whether political pressure shaped reporting, and whether the entire area was covered.

html: Old wood, new fireplace. A wooden beam contains a dated tree ring from 1200 CE, but the building's fireplace was constructed in 1450 CE. Give two reasons the tree-ring date need not establish the fireplace's construction year.
exercises.answer: The building might reuse older timber, and the preserved ring might not be the tree’s outermost ring. The dated growth ring need not correspond to felling, timber placement, or construction.

html: Radiocarbon limits. A charcoal sample is reported as 4,000 BP, uncalibrated. What does BP mean in conventional radiocarbon dating? Why should the archaeologist not simply subtract 4,000 from the current calendar year and announce an exact date?
exercises.answer: Conventional BP uses 1950 as “present.” Radiocarbon years are not identical to calibrated calendar years: atmospheric carbon-14 levels vary, and dating conventions, contamination, and measured uncertainties matter. A 4,000 BP conventional result is not an exact calendar year.

html: Stratigraphic reasoning. A burial pit cuts through layers A and B and contains a coin minted in 1500 CE. The pit was later covered by layer C. What relative ordering can you infer? What can the coin establish and not establish about the burial date?
exercises.answer: The pit is later than the layers it cuts and earlier than the layer sealing it, if the sequence is undisturbed. The coin implies deposition cannot predate minting in 1500, but does not establish whether burial occurred that year or much later. Check for intrusion and reworking.

html: Object versus event. An imported ceramic vessel is found in a port settlement. Give two explanations that do not require its maker or an invading army to have settled there.
exercises.answer: Long-distance trade through intermediaries and a gift or inheritance imported by a traveler are both possible. An object can cross regions without an invading army or permanent migration.

html: Different forms of evidence. For a proposed medieval trade route, name four different kinds of sources that could independently support or complicate the claim.
exercises.answer: Imported goods with secure findspots; price or customs records; merchant correspondence and travel accounts; port infrastructure or shipwreck cargo; coinage and standardized weights; inscriptional evidence. Sources require date and context checks.

groups.title: C. History as a reasoned explanation

html: Causation. Explain the difference between a trigger, a structural condition, and a human decision using a hypothetical political crisis. Do not make up an established historical fact.
exercises.answer: Example: decades of political exclusion create resentment (structural condition), a protest killing sparks demonstrations (trigger), and leaders choose repression rather than negotiation (decision). A responsible analysis specifies a mechanism and alternative choices.

html: The absence of evidence. A village has no surviving records of women owning property. Does that prove no woman ever owned property there? Explain how record preservation and legal categorization might matter.
exercises.answer: No. Records might have been destroyed, property held through arrangements unrecorded by officials, or women classified under household heads. Seek legal cases, wills, contracts, archaeology, and local historical comparison.

html: Magna Carta and its legacy. A speaker says, “In 1215 modern democracy was created in one day.” What is misleading about this claim? Distinguish the charter's immediate political function from later significance.
exercises.answer: Magna Carta addressed specific grievances in a 1215 baronial-royal crisis, not universal modern democratic participation. Its settlement failed and was later reissued and reinterpreted; constitutional legacy developed over centuries.

html: Great Zimbabwe. Explain why the discovery of an imported artifact at Great Zimbabwe would not prove that outsiders built its walls. Name two evidence types that could better evaluate origins.
exercises.answer: An imported artifact may be a trade good. Local architectural sequences, stratigraphy, local pottery and domestic assemblages, radiocarbon evidence, and regional settlement comparisons are better evidence of construction and continuity.

html: Bulgaria's timeline. What specifically distinguishes the constitutional and territorial changes associated with 1878, the unification in 1885, and the independence declaration in 1908? Why are these not synonyms?
exercises.answer: 1878: peace settlements and an autonomous Bulgarian principality under Ottoman suzerainty, with Eastern Rumelia separate. 1885: unification with Eastern Rumelia. 1908: proclamation of full independence, followed by diplomatic recognition. Territory, administrative union, and sovereignty are different questions.

html: Evidence and denial. Explain why an unresolved detail in an eyewitness account does not invalidate an independently corroborated historical event. Use an ethically careful example or a hypothetical case.
exercises.answer: Strong answers distinguish a witness’s fallible recollection of detail from converging archival, material, statistical, and independent testimonial evidence. If sources genuinely corroborate one another, one inconsistency does not overturn the larger event.

html: The disputed quotation. A video attributes a memorable sentence to a historical ruler without naming a source. Outline a six-step verification process and a responsible conclusion if no contemporaneous evidence can be found.
exercises.answer: Identify the earliest known appearance, check historical editions and translations, inspect full context, determine document genre and possible transmission, search specialist literature for attribution, and label the quotation “unverified” if primary support is absent. Do not manufacture an original source.

groups.title: D. Longer essays and source laboratory

html: Essay: causes and responsibility (350–500 words). Choose a historical conflict you know something about. Distinguish the trigger, long-term causes, decisions, and consequences. Show how a causal explanation can coexist with a moral assessment. Identify at least one uncertainty rather than inventing a confident fact.
exercises.answer: Essay rubric: distinct trigger, structural conditions, agents and choices, mechanisms, consequences, and recognition of alternatives. Cite source types accurately and separate explanation of actions from moral approval. Do not pretend that one cause exhausts the explanation.

html: Essay: comparing national memories (350–500 words). Compare a country's commemorative story of a major political event with the questions a historian would ask about treaties, local experiences, and dissenting perspectives. You may use Bulgaria's 1878–1908 history, or another case with verifiable sources.
exercises.answer: Essay rubric: distinguish commemorated date from legal and social processes; include multiple voices and documentary types; discuss whose perspective the national story centers; identify an uncertainty and explain why context enriches rather than erases historical memory.

html: Source laboratory: three imaginary documents. A fictional town suffers a food shortage in 1800. Document A is an official report claiming aid was distributed fairly; Document B is a baker's private letter complaining that flour did not arrive; Document C is a market ledger showing prices rising for six months. Explain what each source can establish, where it might mislead, and what additional evidence could distinguish the competing claims. Treat all three as invented teaching examples.
exercises.answer: A reliably shows what the administration claimed; B records one baker’s report and perspective; C records the observed prices for listed markets and periods. Neither a rising price alone nor one complaint proves universal distribution failure. Seek inventories, delivery receipts, household records, weather and transport evidence, and broader testimony.

html: Your own historical claim audit. Find a factual historical statement in a documentary, social post, museum caption, or textbook. Record its wording; trace it to a credible primary source or scholarly synthesis if possible; explain its limits; and state your confidence. Label anything unverified rather than manufacturing a citation.
exercises.answer: Historical audit rubric: quote the claim, identify who published it and when, find the earliest supporting primary source or serious synthesis, distinguish what it shows from later inference, note alternative explanations and omissions, and assign confidence proportionately. “Not verified” is a legitimate conclusion.

005.title: Practice laboratory
005.answerIntro: These answers model a defensible explanation. Open-ended exercises have multiple possible strong responses; the criteria below explain what good reasoning should include.

html: Map projection. A world map shows Greenland nearly the size of Africa. Explain why this may happen, and name a projection property that would give a fairer comparison of areas.
exercises.answer: Map projections. Mercator preserves local angles but greatly enlarges high-latitude areas. An equal-area projection preserves relative areas, though its shapes may appear distorted.

html: Map scale. A road atlas uses a scale of 1:200,000. Two towns are 7.5 cm apart on the map. Calculate their straight-line ground distance in kilometres, showing the unit conversion.
exercises.answer: Distance at scale. 1:200,000 means 1 cm = 200,000 cm = 2 km. Therefore 7.5 cm × 2 km/cm = 15 km of map-measured straight-line distance.

html: Longitude. Estimate the east-west distance represented by 2° of longitude at latitude 60° N, using 111 km per degree at the Equator and cos(60°) = 0.5.
exercises.answer: Longitude at 60° N. 111 km × cos(60°) ≈ 111 × 0.5 = 55.5 km per degree. Two degrees ≈ 111 km. This uses a spherical approximation.

html: Coordinates. Convert 42°30′ N to decimal degrees. Why is 42.30° N a different point?
exercises.answer: Angular notation. 42°30′ = 42 + 30/60 = 42.5°. The decimal 42.30° = 42.3°, which is 0.2° of latitude (roughly 22 km) farther south.

html: Navigation. Explain the difference between a great-circle route and a rhumb line on a Mercator map. Does a real aircraft always follow the mathematical shortest path?
exercises.answer: Great circle vs rhumb line. A great-circle route is a shortest surface route on an ideal sphere. A rhumb line keeps a constant bearing and appears straight on standard Mercator. Aircraft also account for winds, restrictions, safety and operating costs.

html: Relief. Name the three broad types of plate boundary and give one common geological process associated with each.
exercises.answer: Plate boundaries. Divergent: plates separate and may create new crust. Convergent: plates approach, producing subduction or collision. Transform: plates slide past one another, with earthquakes common along faults.

html: Hazard and disaster. Explain how two places exposed to similar earthquakes could experience radically different human losses.
exercises.answer: Hazard and disaster. Physical shaking alone does not determine losses. Population exposure, building codes, soil conditions, emergency response, inequality and preparedness can strongly alter outcomes.

html: Watershed. Draw two nearby rivers separated by a ridge. Label a drainage divide, a tributary and an outlet. Explain how rainfall on opposite slopes may enter different basins.
exercises.answer: Drainage basin sketch. The ridge is the divide; tributaries flow into a larger channel, whose outlet drains the basin. Rain on opposing slopes may enter different rivers and ultimately different seas.

html: Water politics. Give two potential benefits and two possible concerns associated with a major upstream river dam. Why can a basin map not settle a water-sharing dispute by itself?
exercises.answer: Upstream dam. Possible benefits: hydropower and regulated supply. Possible concerns: altered downstream flows and ecological disruption, including sediment effects. Legal arrangements, data, needs and institutions matter beyond the map.

html: Weather and climate. A town experiences a freezing week during a long-term warming trend. Explain why these observations are not logically inconsistent.
exercises.answer: Weather vs climate. One cold week is a short-term observation; climate describes patterns over many years, including the frequency of cold weeks. A distribution may shift warmer while retaining occasional cold periods.

html: Seasons. Why does the Northern Hemisphere experience summer when the Southern Hemisphere experiences winter? Identify the major cause.
exercises.answer: Seasons. Earth’s axial tilt changes sun angle and daylight duration over the year in opposite hemispheres. Earth–Sun distance is not the primary cause of seasons.

html: Rain shadow. Explain why two settlements on opposite sides of a mountain range might have different rainfall despite being close together.
exercises.answer: Rain shadow. Moist air may rise, cool and precipitate on the windward slope; descending air warms and becomes relatively drier on the leeward side. Wind direction and local weather modify the outcome.

html: Ocean productivity. Explain how a dry coastal region could nevertheless support rich fisheries.
exercises.answer: Dry coast and rich fisheries. Upwelling can bring cold, nutrient-rich water to the surface, supporting phytoplankton and larger food webs. Dry land climates and marine productivity respond to different processes.

html: Trade corridors. Compare straight-line distance and economic distance. Give one example of infrastructure or policy changing the second but not the first.
exercises.answer: Economic distance. Straight-line kilometres are fixed by location; economic distance incorporates travel times, price, infrastructure and institutional barriers. A new bridge or removal of tariffs can reduce it without moving either endpoint.

html: Population density. A district with 900,000 residents covers 30,000 km². Calculate its average density. Why does the result not reveal where residents are concentrated?
exercises.answer: Population density. 900,000 / 30,000 km² = 30 people per km². The average cannot show whether people live throughout the district or cluster in one urban area.

html: Map literacy. A choropleth colours provinces by total reported traffic accidents. List three reasons why it could create a misleading impression about road safety.
exercises.answer: Misleading accident maps. Totals reflect population and traffic exposure; districts vary in area; reporting practices may differ. Suitable rates, road-network data and careful class breaks can improve comparisons.

html: Geographic fallacy. A county has a high average income and a high percentage of cyclists. Does that prove wealthy individuals cycle more? Explain.
exercises.answer: Ecological fallacy. No. District-level correlations do not demonstrate individual-level associations. Individual data, suitable controls and research design would be needed.

html: Climate and geography. Name four influences that can make two places at similar latitudes have different local climates.
exercises.answer: Climate influences. Latitude, altitude, ocean proximity and currents, prevailing winds, topography and continentality are among important influences.

html: Regional reasoning. Explain how the Danube, Balkan Mountains and Black Sea contribute different kinds of geographical opportunity or constraint for Bulgaria.
exercises.answer: Bulgaria. The Danube links inland river networks and forms much of the northern border; the Balkan Mountains influence movement and climate; the Black Sea connects Bulgarian ports to maritime trade. Infrastructure and politics determine outcomes.

html: Causation. Critique this claim: “A landlocked country will always be poor because it has no port.” Provide at least three reasons the claim is too strong.
exercises.answer: Landlocked determinism. Inland trade costs vary with neighbours, railways, customs and institutions. Landlocked states may prosper in high-value services or regional trade. Geography affects costs; it does not alone determine wealth.

html: Case-study comparison. Compare the Nile Basin and the Strait of Malacca. What does each reveal about geographic interdependence, and how do political choices affect outcomes?
exercises.answer: Nile and Malacca. The Nile illustrates shared water-system interdependence across political boundaries. Malacca illustrates commercial networks depending on a constrained maritime passage. Hydrology and navigation do not alone settle political choices.

html: Applied analysis. A company is considering a new warehouse in a mountainous border region. Identify at least six geographical and non-geographical variables it should investigate before committing.
exercises.answer: Warehouse decisions. Check relief, slope and geological hazards; weather; road/rail access; travel time; customs regime; electricity; labour; markets; regulations; land prices; competitors; and environmental effects.

html: Essay. Choose either the Sahel or the Andes. Explain how physical processes, livelihoods, institutions and historical change interact. Include at least one claim that a geographical map alone cannot establish.
exercises.answer: Essay rubric. Use correctly explained physical mechanisms plus people’s livelihoods, institutions and history. Avoid treating the landscape as an inevitable political cause; identify scale, evidence, uncertainty and a plausible counterexample.

html: Independent geographical investigation. Choose a country unfamiliar to you. Write a 500–800-word profile covering location, physical regions, climate, population distribution, connections, hazards, and an important historical or economic question. Cite at least three reputable sources and mark uncertain claims.
exercises.answer: Independent investigation rubric. A strong profile correctly locates the country; separates physical from political data; uses dated, reliable references; describes accessibility and risks; includes a causal question and explicitly flags uncertainty.

006.title: Practice laboratory
006.answerIntro: These answers model a defensible explanation. Open-ended exercises have multiple possible strong responses; the criteria below explain what good reasoning should include.

html: A town records 6 serious crashes over 1.5 million journeys in Year A and 9 over 3 million journeys in Year B. Calculate the crude crashes per million journeys in each year and describe the count and rate changes.
exercises.answer: Road crash rates. Year A: 6/1.5 = 4 crashes per million journeys; Year B: 9/3 = 3 per million. The count rose from 6 to 9 (50%), while the exposure-adjusted rate fell by 25%. Both statements can be true.

html: A survey asks 600 visitors outside one university whether all residents support a graduate tax. Identify the target population, sample, and two important coverage problems.
exercises.answer: University survey. The target is all residents (or other clearly identified relevant population); the sample is 600 university visitors. Nonvisitors lack coverage and visitors may differ by education, age and income. A large sample at one site is not necessarily representative.

html: Explain why adding 2,000 more self-selected responses to a biased online poll does not automatically make it representative.
exercises.answer: More biased responses. Adding observations cannot fix a sampling mechanism that systematically excludes some views. It can reduce random variation among respondents while leaving selection bias intact.

html: Five monthly incomes are €1,000, €1,100, €1,200, €1,300 and €5,400. Calculate the mean and median. Which would better describe a typical worker, and why?
exercises.answer: Mean and median. Total €10,000; mean €10,000/5 = €2,000. Sorted middle is €1,200, the median. The median better describes a typical employee here because one high income pulls up the mean.

html: Store A sells 10 units at €2 average; Store B sells 90 units at €4 average. Calculate the overall unit-weighted mean and the equally weighted mean of store means. Explain which question each answers.
exercises.answer: Weighted and unweighted means. Unit-weighted mean = (10×€2 + 90×€4)/100 = €3.80. Equal-store mean = (€2 + €4)/2 = €3.00. The former answers the average price per unit sold; the latter the average of the two stores’ average prices.

html: Treat 2, 4, 6 and 8 as a population. Calculate its mean and population standard deviation, rounding the latter to two decimals.
exercises.answer: Standard deviation. Mean = (2+4+6+8)/4 = 5. Sum of squared deviations = 9+1+1+9 = 20. Population variance = 20/4 = 5; standard deviation = √5 ≈ 2.24.

html: A chart compares 95 and 100 with bars starting at 94. Explain how the baseline affects the visual ratio and how you would redesign the chart.
exercises.answer: Chart baseline. Above baseline 94, bar heights appear to be 1 and 6; their visual ratio is sixfold even though the measured ratio is 100/95 ≈ 1.053. For a proportional bar comparison, start at zero and label the values; a clearly labeled line chart may show small changes on a nonzero axis.

html: A price index goes from 100 to 125 to 150. Calculate the percentage change in the second period and the total percentage change from the base.
exercises.answer: Index changes. From 125 to 150, the relative change is (150−125)/125 = 20%. From base 100 to 150, it is 50%. The second period also rose 25 index points, which is not a 25% increase.

html: A policy approval figure rises from 20 percent to 25 percent. Express the change in percentage points and as a relative percentage increase.
exercises.answer: Percentage points. 20% to 25% is +5 percentage points. Relative increase = (25−20)/20 × 100 = 25%.

html: A nominal salary rises from €20,000 to €22,000 while an appropriate price index rises from 100 to 110. What is its second-year value in first-year purchasing-power terms?
exercises.answer: Nominal and real salary. €22,000 / (110/100) = €20,000 expressed in first-year purchasing power using this index. Nominal salary increased 10%; price-adjusted salary did not increase in this simplified case.

html: A service sells 100 items in one day and 120 the next. How large is the relative increase? If sales subsequently return from 120 to 100, how large is the relative decrease?
exercises.answer: Asymmetric percentage changes. 100 to 120: (120−100)/100 = 20% increase. 120 back to 100: (100−120)/120 ≈ −16.67%. Percentage changes use the starting value of each movement.

html: Give one plausible confounder behind a positive correlation between city libraries and school achievement. Explain how an experiment might investigate causation.
exercises.answer: Library confounding. Local income or tax revenues could influence library provision and educational opportunities. Random assignment of a suitable library-related intervention to comparable groups, combined with suitable measurement, could help test some causal effects, though there may be ethical or feasibility limits.

html: Within both difficulty groups, Program A exceeds B: difficult A 18/90, B 1/10; easy A 9/10, B 72/90. Compute both overall pass rates and explain the reversal.
exercises.answer: Simpson reversal. Difficult A: 18/90 = 20%, B: 1/10 = 10%; easy A: 9/10 = 90%, B: 72/90 = 80%. Overall A: (18+9)/(90+10) = 27%; B: (1+72)/(10+90) = 73%. A is better within both groups, yet B serves many more easy cases.

html: Why is an area-level relationship between university attendance and election results insufficient to establish how an individual graduate voted?
exercises.answer: Ecological fallacy. Regional education and election figures describe aggregates. They cannot directly establish how individual graduates voted; individual-level evidence and suitable research design are required.

html: In an A/B test with 1,000 visitors per group, A achieves 100 purchases and B 120. Calculate the percentage-point difference and relative improvement. Name one limitation of treating this as final proof.
exercises.answer: A/B test. A = 100/1,000 = 10%; B = 120/1,000 = 12%. Difference = +2 percentage points; relative gain = 2/10 = 20%. Sampling variability, multiple outcomes, poor randomization, changing users or uncertain generalizability may limit conclusions.

html: Under simple-random-sample and normal-approximation assumptions, estimate the 95-percent margin of error when p = 0.5 and n = 400 using 1.96 × sqrt[p(1−p)/n]. Express your answer in percentage points.
exercises.answer: Margin of error 400. 1.96×√(0.5×0.5/400) = 1.96×0.025 = 0.049, or about ±4.9 percentage points. This is only an approximate sampling margin under the stated assumptions.

html: Using the same assumptions, predict the approximate margin if n increases to 1,600. Why does quadrupling the sample, rather than doubling it, approximately halve the margin?
exercises.answer: Margin of error 1600. 1.96×√(0.25/1,600) = 1.96×0.0125 = 0.0245, or ±2.45 points. Standard error scales as 1/√n, so four times the sample gives half the sampling margin.

html: Write a plain-language correction to the statement: “A 95-percent confidence interval proves a 95-percent probability the fixed population proportion lies in this particular interval.”
exercises.answer: Confidence interpretation. A 95% frequentist procedure is designed to cover the fixed population parameter in approximately 95% of repetitions under its assumptions. The level is not generally a posterior probability about this particular fixed parameter after the interval is constructed.

html: Explain why p = 0.03 does not generally mean a three-percent probability that the null hypothesis is true.
exercises.answer: P-value interpretation. p = 0.03 refers to a tail-area probability for results at least as extreme as observed under a specified null model and assumptions. It is not generally the probability that the null is true.

html: With 20 independent tests, each having a five-percent false-positive probability under a true null, compute approximately the probability of at least one false positive: 1 − 0.95^20.
exercises.answer: Multiple testing. 1 − 0.95^20 ≈ 0.6415, or about 64.2%, assuming independent tests and all null hypotheses true. This illustrates a multiple-comparison hazard, not a universal false-discovery percentage.

html: A city reports 800 theft complaints among 100,000 residents, then 960 among 120,000 residents. Calculate complaints per 100,000 in each period and identify one unresolved comparability question.
exercises.answer: Theft rate. First period: 800/100,000 × 100,000 = 800 reports per 100,000. Second: 960/120,000 × 100,000 = 800. Reporting behavior, tourists, commuter exposure, or changing definitions could alter interpretation.

html: A price survey receives no responses from the most expensive ten percent of businesses. Explain why ignoring these missing responses could be dangerous, and why simply inserting the sample mean may not repair the bias.
exercises.answer: Missing expensive businesses. If the missing firms have higher prices, analyzing only respondents may underestimate population prices. Mean imputation assumes missing values resemble observed values and can mask a systematic selection problem.

html: Essay and discussion: A newspaper claims that national living standards are improving because GDP increased. Prepare an evidence-based response that distinguishes aggregate output, population, inflation, distribution and other dimensions of wellbeing.
exercises.answer: Living standards essay rubric. Distinguish total and per-capita real GDP; inspect price changes, household median income, distribution, poverty, services, housing and health. Explain how data are measured, give uncertainty, and avoid assuming national output directly describes every resident’s circumstances.

html: Independent investigation: Find one real publicly available chart about population, science, economics or politics. Write a 300–500-word audit of the original source, variables, denominators, timescale, graph design, uncertainty and at least two plausible interpretations. Do not claim causation from correlation alone.
exercises.answer: Chart-audit investigation rubric. A strong audit identifies original source, date, question, variable definitions, sampling/coverage, denominator, scale, selection effects, graph design, uncertainty and at least two plausible explanations. It clearly distinguishes observation from causal inference.

007.title: Practice laboratory
007.answerIntro: These answers model a defensible explanation. Open-ended exercises have multiple possible strong responses; the criteria below explain what good reasoning should include.

html: Define a system in your own words. Explain why simply listing its components does not reveal how it behaves.
exercises.answer: What makes a system. A system is a collection of interacting elements whose relationships generate behavior. A list of personnel, machines and money cannot explain outcomes without showing the flows, feedback and rules that connect them.

html: For a hospital, suggest a sensible system boundary for investigating waiting times. Name two outside factors your boundary might miss.
exercises.answer: Hospital boundary. Include arrivals, triage, clinicians, staffed beds, patient movement, discharges and scheduling. Ambulance availability, national hiring regulations or a regional outbreak could fall outside a narrow hospital boundary but affect waiting.

html: Distinguish an event, pattern and structure using recurring school absenteeism as your example.
exercises.answer: Event-pattern-structure. Event: 50 students absent on Tuesday. Pattern: absences rise every winter or around examinations. Structure: transport reliability, infectious disease, schedules, incentives and reporting rules could contribute. Investigate, do not assume.

html: A reservoir contains 1,000 cubic metres of water. Each week 80 arrive and 110 leave. Assuming constant rates, calculate the amount after four weeks.
exercises.answer: Reservoir stock. 1,000 + 4 × 80 − 4 × 110 = 880 cubic metres. The weekly net loss is 30 cubic metres; rates are assumed unchanged and no other flows included.

html: A shop has 300 items and receives 70 a day while selling 90 a day. How many items remain after five days if there are no other flows?
exercises.answer: Shop inventory. 300 + 5 × 70 − 5 × 90 = 200 items. A positive sales flow may coexist with a declining inventory stock.

html: Explain why a region could reduce the annual number of emigrants without immediately reversing its population decline.
exercises.answer: Migration and demographic inertia. Reduced emigration is a smaller outflow, not necessarily a net population gain. Births, deaths, immigration and population age structure continue to affect the stock for years.

html: Draw or describe the reinforcing feedback between marketplace buyers and sellers. Give two limits that could weaken the loop.
exercises.answer: Marketplace reinforcing loop. More buyers attract sellers; more sellers expand selection; greater selection attracts buyers. Platform fees, congestion, fraud, limited markets or competing platforms can weaken the loop.

html: Explain why “reinforcing” does not necessarily mean beneficial and “balancing” does not necessarily mean desirable.
exercises.answer: Loop labels are descriptive. Reinforcing means amplifying an existing movement; a rumor spiral can be harmful and a learning network beneficial. Balancing means resisting change; it can stabilize helpful or harmful arrangements.

html: A heater turns on whenever temperature falls below a set point and turns off after reaching it. Identify the balancing loop and its target.
exercises.answer: Thermostat. Room temperature below the set point activates heating. Heating raises temperature; once the target is reached, the signal for additional heat falls. Target: thermostat set temperature.

html: A retailer orders 50 boxes on Monday despite having 50 in stock, then orders 50 more daily until a delayed delivery arrives. Describe one mechanism that could produce overstocking.
exercises.answer: Delayed overordering. When orders already placed are not counted as incoming inventory, the manager sees an unchanged stock and repeats orders. Arrivals bunch after the delay and may exceed demand; accurate pipeline information can reduce overshoot.

html: Why might a road near capacity experience sharply increased delays from only a modest increase in traffic?
exercises.answer: Nonlinear congestion. Near capacity, queues interact with junctions or service times; small additions to traffic can produce much larger increases in waiting. Exact effects depend on the specific network.

html: A bakery mixes 400 loaves per hour, bakes 120 and packages 200. Assuming the stages operate together without other constraints, what is the approximate maximum steady throughput? Why?
exercises.answer: Bakery bottleneck. Maximum steady output is about 120 loaves per hour because the oven is the slowest of the three stated stages (400, 120, 200). Faster mixing alone does not raise oven throughput.

html: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of keeping larger inventory buffers in a retail store.
exercises.answer: Buffers trade-off. Advantages: stockouts are less likely during uncertain supply or demand. Disadvantages: inventory holds cash, requires space and may spoil. Optimal inventory depends on lead times, costs and risk.

html: Describe the common-pool-resource dilemma in a fishery and explain why it does not prove that community management must fail.
exercises.answer: Commons institutions. Each fisher can gain by taking more despite harm to future stock. Monitoring, credible collective rules, graduated sanctions and local participation can help manage common-pool resources; failure is not inevitable.

html: Explain the ice–albedo feedback and why the diagram alone cannot tell you the amount of future warming.
exercises.answer: Ice-albedo reasoning. Warming can reduce reflective snow and ice, exposing darker surfaces that absorb more solar energy and amplify warming. Total warming depends on forcing, other feedback, regional conditions and physical measurements.

html: In an intentionally simplified hypothetical model with an effective reproduction number of 1.5 held constant, what are the expected generation counts after two generations starting from 100 cases? State a limitation.
exercises.answer: Simple reproduction arithmetic. Starting with 100 infections, after one generation expected infections are 150, and after two 225, in a simplified constant-R model. Real infections are stochastic and susceptibility, contacts and interventions change.

html: A city sees high rents, then authorizes buildings that will open in three years. Identify two ways that delay could complicate future housing outcomes.
exercises.answer: Construction delay. New homes may arrive after demand has slowed, creating possible vacancies; meanwhile high prices persist while permits and construction proceed. Financing and developer expectations matter.

html: Explain the security dilemma with a causal chain. Give one condition that may reduce the spiral.
exercises.answer: Security dilemma. A worries → A arms → B perceives threat → B arms → A worries more. Transparency, verifiable defensive postures, communication or agreements may reduce uncertainty; aggression and deterrence still need contextual assessment.

html: A firm rewards workers solely for the number of sales, and average discounts rise sharply. Suggest how the metric may have changed behavior and name a more balanced evaluation approach.
exercises.answer: Sales incentive. Workers rewarded for unit sales may discount aggressively, raising volume but lowering margin. Balance sales targets with gross profit, returns, customer satisfaction and transparent review of unintended behaviors.

html: Explain rebound effects using more energy-efficient equipment; distinguish reduced energy per use from total energy consumption.
exercises.answer: Rebound effect. Efficiency lowers energy per use, but a lower cost can increase frequency or intensity of use. Total energy depends on both efficiency and usage changes; rebound may be partial and its size must be measured.

html: Give two plausible interventions for recurring school overcrowding: one directed at an immediate symptom, and one at an underlying structure.
exercises.answer: Overcrowding responses. Immediate: temporary rooms or changed timetables. Structural: demographic forecasts, school construction, transport redesign and staffing policy. Compare time horizon, cost and equity.

html: Design a five-variable causal map for stockouts in a small supermarket. Label at least one reinforcing or balancing loop and one delay.
exercises.answer: Five-variable map. Example: demand (+) → sales (+) → inventory depletion (+) → stockouts (−) → satisfaction (−) → demand; delayed deliveries feed stock recovery. Name signs carefully and consider outstanding orders and product mix.

html: A new public policy is announced as a solution to unemployment. In 250–350 words, propose a systems audit that names affected actors, one stock, two flows, a possible unintended effect and evidence needed to judge outcomes.
exercises.answer: Unemployment policy audit. A credible answer names workers, employers, public agencies and taxpayers; employment stock, hiring and separation flows; skill-training or hiring delays; possible displacement or wage effects; baseline data and credible comparison. It should distinguish claims of causality from before–after trends.

html: A government claims that expanding one airport will automatically reduce all regional transport costs. Identify at least four reasons this claim requires more evidence before acceptance.
exercises.answer: Airport expansion claim. More capacity may not address rail links, airport fees, labor shortages or connecting services. Demand may adapt; environmental and taxpayer costs matter; some routes may lose service. Need network and cost evidence rather than the word automatically.

html: Compare two hypothetical approaches to water shortages: expanding reservoir capacity versus reducing losses in the water network. Discuss short- and long-term effects, costs, delays and who might bear the burdens.
exercises.answer: Water shortage comparison. Storage may create a buffer but needs capital, land, time and ecological review. Leak reduction can preserve existing supply but requires measurement and repairs; efficacy depends on loss type and network. Both have distributional and maintenance implications.

html: Independent investigation: Choose an actual system (public transport, a local business, an energy network or a public institution). Create a one-page diagram and a 400–600-word evidence-based explanation of its behavior over time, then state what observation would falsify one arrow in your map.
exercises.answer: Independent investigation rubric. A strong submission defines its outcome and period; draws evidence-grounded stocks, flows and feedback; cites observation sources; proposes at least one rival explanation and a measurement that could disconfirm one arrow; distinguishes ethical evaluation from causal explanation.

008.title: Practice laboratory
008.answerIntro: These answers model a defensible explanation. Open-ended exercises have multiple possible strong responses; the criteria below explain what good reasoning should include.

html: Explain in your own words why recognizing a paragraph during rereading is not the same as recalling it in conversation.
exercises.answer: Familiarity versus recall Rereading provides cues and recognition; conversation requires reconstructing ideas without the page. Successful recall and explanation are stronger evidence of retrievable learning.

html: Design a three-day schedule to retain the terms 'latitude,' 'longitude,' and 'map projection' without simply rereading their definitions repeatedly.
exercises.answer: Three-day practice Day 1: read and explain the terms; day 2: answer prompts without notes and correct errors; day 3: draw an unlabeled coordinate grid or explain one projection from memory. The exact spacing can be adjusted.

html: Take a topic from this book and write one factual flashcard, one 'why' question, and one application problem. Explain why each tests something different.
exercises.answer: Three learning prompts Example: fact “What does latitude measure?”; explanation “Why does longitude distance vary with latitude?”; application “Estimate distance for one degree of latitude.” These target distinct skills.

html: Describe one situation where interleaving related material might help and one where focused practice is probably more suitable.
exercises.answer: Interleaving Useful after initial learning when deciding among related chart types or map concepts; more focused practice helps when the core idea is unfamiliar or a beginner is overwhelmed.

html: Propose an error-log entry for confusing the median and the mean, including a short worked example.
exercises.answer: Mean and median error log Example data: 2, 3, 100. Mean is 35, median is 3. Note the error: mistook the arithmetic average for the middle ordered observation. Reattempt with a different skewed set.

html: Essay and discussion. Design a sustainable weekly general-knowledge routine for someone who works, enjoys gaming, and has only thirty minutes available most days. Include a way to track whether the knowledge is retained.
exercises.answer: Essay: sustainable routine A realistic plan has recurring short sessions, meaningful stopping rules for gaming, a weekly quiz, spaced reviews, one open-ended explanation, and flexibility around missed days. Success is durable recall and control, not pages completed.

009.title: Practice laboratory
009.answerIntro: These answers model a defensible explanation. Open-ended exercises have multiple possible strong responses; the criteria below explain what good reasoning should include.

html: Reconstruction: Explain why a branching tree is a better model of human evolution than a ladder. Use chimpanzees and Neanderthals as examples, and be precise about ancestry versus relatedness.
exercises.answer: Reconstruction. A branching tree allows contemporaneous lineages. Chimpanzees and modern humans share ancestral populations; chimpanzees are not our ancestors. Neanderthals were related human relatives who lived alongside and sometimes interbred with Homo sapiens, not an intermediate rung.

html: Evidence and inference: What does a 3.6-million-year-old footprint tell us? Name two conclusions it supports and two things it cannot establish without additional evidence.
exercises.answer: Footprints. Laetoli strongly supports upright bipedal locomotion and the presence of hominins in that place about 3.6 million years ago. The tracks alone cannot identify language, beliefs, intentions, or the individual walkers with absolute certainty.

html: Dating: A pigment image is covered by a mineral deposit dated to 40,000 years ago. What is the logically justified statement about the age of the painting? What would you need to establish a maximum age?
exercises.answer: Dating a covered painting. If a mineral layer formed over the image 40,000 years ago, the painting is at least 40,000 years old (assuming the deposit is truly on top and correctly dated). A securely dated underlying layer may constrain an older boundary; careful stratigraphic context is essential.

html: Technology: Why is it wrong to say that Homo sapiens invented the first stone tools? Distinguish evidence of tool manufacture from identification of the maker.
exercises.answer: Toolmakers. Lomekwi tools date to about 3.3 million years ago, far older than Homo sapiens. Stone artifacts show deliberate flaking or battering; naming the maker requires separate evidence and may remain uncertain.

html: Migration arithmetic: If the edge of a population's range shifts an average of 1.5 kilometers every 30 years, how far would it shift in 18,000 years? Why must the answer not be presented as a real measured migration speed?
exercises.answer: Migration illustration. 18,000/30 = 600 generations of thirty-year intervals in the hypothetical rate model; 600 × 1.5 km = 900 km. This is arithmetic illustrating a slow geographic range shift, not a measured movement rate or actual route for an ancient population.

html: Geography: Why did low Pleistocene sea levels make some migration routes easier but not eliminate the maritime challenge of reaching Sahul?
exercises.answer: Sahul geography. Lower sea levels united some islands and joined Australia to New Guinea, but a continuous land bridge did not link Sunda to Sahul. Crossing water remained necessary; the specific vessels and routes are not directly preserved.

html: Genetics: Explain in three sentences what Neanderthal-derived ancestry demonstrates and name one important fact it cannot reveal about an individual ancient encounter.
exercises.answer: Neanderthal ancestry. Patterns of ancient and modern DNA demonstrate mixing among at least some Homo sapiens and Neanderthal populations. Some descendants inherited segments of Neanderthal ancestry. Genetics cannot reveal the motive, consent, or emotional experience of a particular ancient encounter.

html: Source criticism: A headline reads, 'New Footprints Prove Exactly When the First Americans Arrived.' Identify at least three problems with this wording and rewrite it responsibly.
exercises.answer: Footprint headline.
